slides.title: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) tests
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · What it is used for · 1/3
bullets: Specimen: Stool (antigen or PCR), breath samples (urea breath test) or a biopsy taken at endoscopy

What it is used for: The tests show whether H. pylori is causing digestive symptoms and whether treatment has cleared it. Signs of gastritis or an ulcer include upper belly pain, bloating, feeling full too soon, nausea and vomiting, burping, loss of appetite and weight loss. Black, tarry stool, blood or "coffee grounds" in vomit, or sudden severe pain need urgent care.

slides.title: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) tests
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · What it is used for · 2/3
bullets: Physiology: H. pylori is a common bacterium that infects the lining of the stomach and the first part of the small intestine; most people never have symptoms. It is the most common cause of peptic ulcers and causes gastritis; untreated H. pylori gastritis increases the chance of stomach cancer. It may spread through vomit, stool or saliva, and through contaminated food and water.

slides.title: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) tests
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · What it is used for · 3/3
bullets: Methods: the urea breath test — you swallow urea "labeled" with a special carbon atom; if H. pylori is present it turns the urea into carbon dioxide and the label appears in exhaled breath (samples before and after are compared). Stool tests detect H. pylori antigen (the most common test) or genetic material by PCR. When other tests are not enough, a biopsy is taken at endoscopy (rapid urease test, culture).

slides.title: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) tests
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Interpreting the result
cols: A positive result means H. pylori infection. The provider usually prescribes one or more antibiotics plus medicines to help the stomach heal; after treatment the test may be repeated to confirm the bacteria are gone.
A negative (normal) result means you probably do not have H. pylori infection; other tests may be ordered to find the cause of symptoms.

slides.title: Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) tests
slides.eyebrow: Stool and parasitology · Pre-analytics and interferences
bullets: Pre-analytics: You may need to stop certain medicines for two weeks to a month before testing, including many taken for the symptoms — tell your provider everything you take. Stool is collected in a clean, dry container without urine, water or toilet paper. Fasting for several hours is needed before endoscopy.

Limitations: Blood antibody tests for H. pylori are not commonly used for diagnosis because they cannot tell an active infection from a past one. A negative antibody result, though, usually means there was no infection when the blood was taken.

In gastrointestinal diseases – the significance and laboratory diagnosis of H. pylori?
bullets: 1. H. pylori is a gram-negative spiral bacterium of the gastric mucosa; associated with chronic gastritis, peptic ulcer, gastric adenocarcinoma and the risk of MALT lymphoma.

2. Non-invasive tests: 13C-urease breath test (the most reliable for active infection and for checking eradication), stool monoclonal antigen test (active infection), serology (IgG) – shows past exposure, does not assess active infection or treatment outcome.
3. Invasive (endoscopic) tests: rapid urease test, histology, culture and antibiotic susceptibility, PCR (clarithromycin resistance mutations).

slides.title: In gastrointestinal diseases – the significance and laboratory diagnosis of H. pylori?
bullets: 4. Preanalytics: stop PPIs ≥2 weeks, antibiotics and bismuth preparations ≥4 weeks (except for serology) – otherwise false negatives.
5. Confirming eradication: ≥4 weeks after finishing treatment – UBT or stool antigen; serology is not used for this purpose.
